utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So buenos dias. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All the accused are here. I think I also see a full house on the Defence teams. I don't see anyone's absence. And the Prosecution team, it's the same, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. And I think we can start. Present for today's sitting is the representative of the US Embassy, Ms. Schildge, and I don't see the Defence experts. None of them is present. Okay. Good morning to you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not going to straightaway with the first of the cross-examinations, because the week starts with a very good piece of excellent news. Mr. Haynes. For Mr. Haynes, January 2008 brings the much-aspired-for silk is being made, Queen's Counsel, and the news has just arrived. It's a great honour for Mr. Haynes, a well-deserved honour, I must say, but it's also an honour for all of us, being able to work with Mr. Haynes and see the dexterity with which he fulfils his task as a Defence lawyer for his client. I'm sure that your team and the other Defence teams and the Prosecution join me in congratulating you on this great honour that you have received, Mr. Haynes, and that we, my country and many others, we say, "[foreign language spoken]," you will go far, you will go far. So that's it. I think we can -- also I must put on record that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today. Judge Stole couldn't be with us. He will join us later on, if he can, but it is not very likely. Now, before we start, let's have a re-revision of the estimated cross-examination time. Mr. Haynes now being a QC, will reduce -- will cut down on his estimated cross-examination, but I'll come to him at the end. Mr. Zivanovic, you had asked for five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For the time being, I cannot reduce my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm making it clear that this will, however long it will take, it's not going to reduce or move by one inch the other time limits and dates that we have established. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I still have five hours, I believe. I'll work hard to try to reduce it somewhat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I had asked for four hours. I had changed that to five hours, rather than the six that were expected last week, and I hope to be able to reduce that to maybe the four. But I need, at this moment, the five hours requested. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I believe I was very realistic about our cross-examination time. It's going to be two hours, and I will stick to this estimation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I need eight hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We took the opportunity yesterday to discuss the topics of cross-examination that people were going to employ, and it seemed to me that what was ahead of me left me with only three or four very specific areas to cross-examine Mr. Butler about. My estimate is very pessimistic, but I'm conscious of the fact that those ahead of me, perhaps in light of my new status, have prevailed upon me to pick up anything they miss out ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Let's start with Mr. -- Oh, I'm sorry. Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad you gave Mr. Haynes precedence over me today, but, Your Honour, notwithstanding that, we stick by our day estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Four hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam, I don't know how this is going to work for you, because there will be areas that are of interest to you and areas that are definitely not, and our experience here is that the time estimate is usually erratic. So I don't know what to tell you, but if I could ask counsel to restrict -- or to put the questions that Ms. Schildge would be interested in or is here for at the beginning of your cross-examination, that would help her not spending too much time out of her office and in the courtroom here. Can we agree on this? Okay. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and together with my colleague, Ms. Mira Tapuskovic, I appear on behalf of Vujadin Popovic in this case. You have studied the Rules of Service for the securities services which were in force in Serbia as of July 1995 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction "in the VRS."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with Article 477. I'm sure that you've gone through the Rules on a number of occasions, and I'm particularly interested in Item 6 and 7, which regulate the tasks of security services. You may want to refresh your recollection concerning those articles, and I will gladly give you an opportunity to do so, since most of my questions will have to do with those. I apologise. The figure should have been "407."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have them available right before you now, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I have no reference material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because, I mean, there is no point in proceeding unless you have these available. Who is going to provide them? They are on e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: E-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then the reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It is P407, pages 11 and -- actually, paragraphs 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to scroll to the next page in English, please, so I could read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among all the tasks listed, did you find any particular one which will have to do with POWs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, there is no specific task with respect to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you saw that in paragraph 6, there are tasks listed and that it is said that security organs are to implement those tasks. First of all, do you agree with me that this is concerning counter-intelligence measures that you addressed in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The issues that you have listed in this particular paragraph 6 are reflective of the counter-intelligence role, although I'll note it again in 6(f) there is issues in respect to analysing and data and intelligence reporting, but again that reflects more along the lines of their view of counter-intelligence reporting as opposed to battlefield information, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is your understanding of the expression that the security organs are responsible for? Does it mean that, in your understanding, they are independent in executing those tasks and that they do not receive orders from their unit commander in that regard?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in which regard, in the counter-intelligence function or within the general purpose of -- okay, in the counter-intelligence function, the unit commanders, for the most part, do not play a substantial role, as I understand the regulations. The direction on counter-intelligence functions comes as a result of the type of specialised technical guidance and management that would come from higher security organs. So with respect to counter-intelligence and related roles, no, I do not believe that the unit commander of which that security officer works for plays a definitive role.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, in your view, that the tasks listed and that the security organs are responsible for are such that would fall only under their competence, i.e., that no one apart from those organs can execute them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. For example, looking back at this particular regulation in both 6 and 7, it does discuss the fact that they prepare or propose tasks for the military police. In that view, they are in fact, you know, working as part of a cooperative or collaborative effort within the Command to propose those steps for the commander to either adopt, you know, decline, or modify as he sees fit. So it's not a complete isolation within that respect. In large part, it depends upon the specific task of the security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I may have been insufficiently precise. I only had in mind the counter-intelligence tasks. Can those tasks be executed only by security organs or by some other services or branches?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, in the regulations, is some discussion with respect to collaboration with the intelligence branch along this line. However, within the strict confines of the counter-intelligence mission, the security officer proceeds on that independently, getting direction from his -- his specialty branch, the security branch. The commander does not have a role in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can they revert those tasks to another, to someone else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who is "they"? Can the security officer delegate his tasks?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Security organs.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't think that by regulation they could delegate counter-intelligence tasks to other organs of the Command in so much as make them responsible for the completion of that. Would other organs of the Command have a role? Again, depending on the situation. You know, if information came that an officer on the Command Staff was potentially a security -- a major security threat or risk, you know, the security officer may choose to bring in the unit commander, inform him of that fact, so that concrete steps can be taken to either remove that officer from a position where he could potentially violate trust or to take some other measures. But as for the absolute -- you know, abrogating that responsibility to say, you know, the commander is responsible for counter-intelligence strictly or the intelligence branch is responsible strictly, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These counter-intelligence tasks conducted by the security organs, do you believe them to be of importance for the armed forces, especially at times of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the denial of pertinent information to an opposing force is always a primary objective of any armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason due to which instruction -- a directive on the part of the General Staff was issued, stipulating that 80 per cent of their time they should dedicate to the counter-intelligence tasks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that's a -- that would be a fair assumption, given the fact that with the presence of not only opposing forces but of the international forces that were, in some cases, you know, involved in, you know, actions between the three warring parties, yes, the denial of pertinent information would have been of high importance to the Main Staff and, you know, in fact, you know, could have been the justification for the publication of that instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask to clarify some of the answers you gave to the Prosecutor concerning the military police. At page 19636, lines 22 to 24, you said, by way of response, that a military police unit is commanded by an officer of a higher formation within which that particular military police unit is a part of. My question is: Does the military police unit itself have its own commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And he is subordinated to the commander of the unit, the part of which that military police unit is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have explained that the security organ makes proposals to the commander as to how to use the military police unit. Do you agree that the commander need not accept such proposals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the commander can make his own decision on the use of the military police unit without prior proposals having been given by the security organs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and, you know, not only do I agree, I believe that for large part, the military documents that we've analysed reflect that that is what happened, you know, in a practical aspect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You probably went through the rules of the military police as well and you've familiarised yourself with their tasks, and I wanted to ask you about one particular task. Therefore, we would have to go to 707, P707, this being the rules of the military police, page 13. Please have a look at one particular task, since there is a number of them here. It would be task 25(f).

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, it's not up on my screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat? (25)(f), sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says the military police should take part in directing the movements of refugees and uncovering any members of enemy units who have infiltrated the refugees?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked by the Prosecutor whether, among the refugees in Potocari, there were able-bodied men. It was page 19822, line 20, on the 16th of January. Can you tell me whether you include in that category of able-bodied men those who, according to the laws and regulations, were obliged to take part in the defence of their country?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the men who were between age 15 and 60 who were in Potocari, then those would fall within the category of able-bodied men that the military police and other police organs would have been separating, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you studied regulations, the regulations of the former Yugoslavia and the warring parties, could you please tell me whether the regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina regulated that those persons were duty-bound to defend their country?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question, in so much as while I may have looked at those particular regulations many years ago, I cannot tell you, back from memory, whether that was the case. I assume, like all of the warring parties, that there were mandatory military call-ups that would cover those individuals, but I can't give you specifics of the regulations, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and jog your memory by showing you another document, which is 1D504. This is a decree on defence which was passed by Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 20th of May, 1992. I'm not sure whether this has been translated or not, but I'm going to read to you Article 51 on page six. Article 51 reads as follows: "The right and obligation to be trained for defence belongs under the conditions prescribed by the law to the citizens ranging between 15 and 60 years of age for men and 55 years of age for women if they are able to follow such training. According to the provisions of this decree law, this obligation excludes pregnant women, women with children under the age of seven, and all those who are not able to follow this training." Can you tell me, please, did you ever have an opportunity to see or read this decree law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you absolutely, it's been a while, but I am familiar with the general thrust of where you're going with it. I certainly don't doubt that it's not authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a very concrete question now, more concrete than the one that was posed to you by the Prosecutor. Do you have any information that in Potocari, among the refugees, there were members of the BiH Army as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only documentary information that I have reflects to the 17 July and 18 July Bratunac reports with respect to wounded Muslims who were evacuated from Bratunac, with the exception of one member who was listed as a war crimes list -- or on the war crimes list, and I believe he is being associated with being a military member. That's why he's on that war crimes list. The other information that I have, with respect to my knowledge of the various videos of Potocari and the pictures of the individuals within that, there may very well be men who are wearing various elements of military uniforms. Whether that was their only clothing or whether they were, in fact, military members, you know, because there's no documents reflecting that, I don't know. I'm willing to assume, for the purposes, that, you know, there would be some soldiers there who donned civilian clothes because they wanted to remain with their families rather than trek through the woods pursuant to their duty. But, you know, I don't know that as a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are speculating, basically. You think it was possible, but you're not -- you don't have any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no evidence one way or another. I'm sure it's possible, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's -- from your investigations, as they have been put, you haven't come across such evidence, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other than the one specific thing that I've indicated, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's move, and try to avoid any speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to look at 1D463. I am not sure whether that document has been translated, again. This is an interim report issued by the General Staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated 12th July 1995. It was dispatched at 1325 hours to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can the document be scrolled down a little, please. Thank you very much. This is excellent. You say that the document describes what happened in Srebrenica. I'm not going to go through the entire document, in order to avoid wasting time. In the penultimate paragraph, in the second sentence from the bottom, I'm going to read that, because it's very characteristic. It says here: "Last night, around 2300 hours, we had between 15 and 20.000 refugees who were sitting in the area of war responsibilities together with 300 fighters of the BiH Army in the Potocari camp." Am I right in saying that among the refugees who were in the Potocari camp, there were also fighters of the BiH Army; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, based on this document, and again I'm willing to conclude that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did you have an occasion to read reports on Srebrenica that the members of the Dutch-Bat provided to the Dutch government on their return from that mission, the so-called "Srebrenica debriefing," which is a collection -- a rather large collection of their statements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I read with respect to the Dutch debriefing on Srebrenica was one that was published in, I believe, late 1995, and I have referenced it as part of my analytical narrative. If there is a follow-on larger Dutch document with respect to, you know, just all of their witness statements, I may have reviewed it, but because again it's based primarily on witness information, it wouldn't have been something I would have included in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Kindly look at another document, which is 1D39. This is a statement which was provided during the investigation on Srebrenica by Major Franken, who was the deputy commander of the Dutch-Bat, and I'm sure you will remember that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I know of Major Franken and I am aware of his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 7. In the English version, you will find the relevant part in the third paragraph, where it says: "After the refugees had left ..." And the reference is made to the refugees from the white house, from Bela Kuca, the Serbs in blue uniforms set fire to the houses, which were around the house, during which a considerable amount of small arms ammunition exploded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this indicate that among the refugee belongings, there was also ammunition that had been left lying around Bela Kuca?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking in consideration, you know, if this is in fact, you know, an issue noted by Major Franken and it's accurate, it would reflect that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, it says that the witness heard that after the refugees had left, a number of weapons had been found. My question to you, sir, is this: You did not use this information in your reports, i.e., in your account of Srebrenica; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct, sir, I didn't use this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this because you were not familiar with this or because you considered all this irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it's because, as a matter of practice in my reporting, as I've indicated in my reports, I was not prepared to be put in a position where I would be cross-examined on information that was derived from a witness who, by his position, would be testifying before this Tribunal. So within that broader context, my goal has always been only to use witness-based information when it was absolutely necessary to set the context of a particular event, so my other analysis with respect to documents and with respect to other intercepts would make sense. The omission of witness statements by almost all of the parties involved was by design. It was not by a lack of awareness or any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you please tell me whether you had information that the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Srebrenica, had ordered everybody to leave Srebrenica on the 10th of July or, rather, on the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did, and that is included in my report, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, everybody had to obey that order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they had to obey it or not, I can't say, but the practical effect is that it was obeyed for its entirety when the VRS arrived in Srebrenica on the 11th. The town -- with the exception of wounded, the town was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your examination-in-chief, you were shown an order with respect to Krivaja 1995, dated 2nd of July 1995. This is Prosecutor's Exhibit number 107, and it was an order for that military operation. I would like to ask you a general question first. This order, does it have all the elements that the military doctrine considers to be standard for this type of military operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, that is correct. I am aware that the air defence portion of this order was published, I believe, on the 5th, and there may have been some additional logistical annexes that may have been published. However, you know, on its face, this is a fairly complete, by-the-book type of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, when we look at bullet point number 1, actually, when we summarise that bullet point, we see that it says here that the enemy had launched a general offensive in the territory of Republika Srpska, conducting attacks targeting units of the Drina Corps. Further on, there is an estimate of further enemy activities, and then a conclusion that over the past several days, Muslim forces had been very active in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. It says further on that they -- that the sabotage groups and terrorist groups had been infiltrating in order to attack and torch unprotected villages, kill civilian population, and that there were also smaller units around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. And it also says that they are trying especially hard to link up the enclaves and open a corridor to Kladanj. According to your estimate, would that be a fair representation of the situation that prevailed at the moment? If you look at the order, would this be a good reflection of the situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, from the perspective or understanding of the Drina Corps, I believe this is a very fair representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're saying that this is from the perspective of the Drina Corps and that this is a fair representation of the situation. What about you? As a military expert, would you say that, from your perspective, that would be a fair representation? In the course of your analysis, did you come across any documents that would corroborate this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that I came across in large part substantiate the fact that the Bosnian Muslim forces of the 28th Division and of the Zepa enclave were engaged in raids outside those areas for the purpose of tying down VRS forces. Whether or not, again, they would actually be able to physically link up the enclaves, in the sense of one homogeneous area, they never had the combat power to do that. So, again, I believe, like I said, from the Drina Corps' perspective of the information that they were receiving, it's a fair reflection of that situation, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to look at the Muslim documents dating from that time, i.e., the time which preceded the passing of the order for active combat, dated 2nd July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did look at a number of those Muslim military documents both preceding the beginning of the Krivaja 1995 operation as well as after it started. So I have seen those documents, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then you must have seen in these documents that the defence of Srebrenica had started on the 26th of June, 1995, some week or so before the order for active combat was passed. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm a bit confused by your question. The defence of Srebrenica from -- from whom? Was it the Muslims defending Srebrenica or was it the Serbs who were defending the borders of the enclave from Srebrenica? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will explain this on a document that I'm going to show you. The number is 1D648. The page is number 17. We can also look at the first page. This is a list of combat activities carried out in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps between 1992 and 1995. If you look at the last page -- can we please see the last page of the document. This was signed by General Sead Delic, who was the commander of the 2nd Corps. If we can go back a page. So this is page number 17. I would kindly ask you to show us page number 16 of this document. Sixteen, page 16, please. It seems that this page is missing, of all pages, but I'm sure we'll be able to locate it. Can this please be placed on the ELMO. Can we look at that page together, operation under number 619, this is what I'm interested in. Under number 619, it says: "Defence of Srebrenica," the type of military operation, and the last column indicates the duration of this operation, which started on the 26th of June and ended on 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If Mr. Butler is going to be asked to comment on a 17-page report, if we could at least have just something about the first 1 through 15, because I don't know this document myself, I don't know if it's an entire list of material or anything, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I think it's a legitimate comment. Do we have a hard copy of it available?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Hard copies in e-court, but just this page was omitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But in e-court, it doesn't serve us any good if it's a multiple page that has to be consulted from time to time. Is it available in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can see that this is a large list, beginning in 1992, but is there a cover page, is there something to put it in context, I mean, something besides just a list? I mean, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. McCloskey. I can't help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I found this document in e-court, and it is the whole document. I'm not aware that there is some part of this document not published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're saying this is a list of combat activities carried out in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And it was made by the commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but the last page, you will see this is signed by General Sead Delic, who was the commander of the 2nd Corps. And then you refer him to page 17 and then to page 16. Then there is a missing page. But I am completely at a loss, like Mr. McCloskey and I suppose also like my colleagues. I can't help you, Mr. McCloskey. I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If that's all there is, I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. When is it dated? When did Delic allegedly sign this and date this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I found this document at the EDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, it says here that the defence of Srebrenica started on the 26th of June, 1995. In a nutshell, much before than the order for combat activity of Krivija 1995 was ever passed; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the operation before that, number 618. It says here: "Attack on Visnjica" which was carried out on the 25th of June, 1995. Do you know where Visnjica is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not off the top of my head, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to refresh your memory. Let us look at P428. It is a Prosecution exhibit. This is the situation report of the 28th Division of the Army of B and H from Srebrenica, dated the 30th of June, 1995. Have you had an occasion to see this report before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I may have. I couldn't tell you absolutely whether I did or did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 38th of June [as interpreted], and that's what it should read in the transcript. I apologise, the 30th of June, the 30th of June. In item 1 it says the soldiers of the 28th Division decided to contribute as much as possible to the efforts of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in their fight against the aggressor, thus increasing their activity in the temporarily-occupied territory. Did you see that part of the report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The temporarily-occupied territory is referred to with the acronym "TPZT" in the document. What is referred to here is the territory that was controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, it is stated that 13 Chetniks were killed, that some weapons were seized, and I won't go through all of it, but is your understanding here that the 13 Chetniks killed were actually soldiers of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have no way of knowing whether they were all soldiers or not. Again, when you were asking me the initial question about where it was, I was kind of hoping you'd put a map up there. I'm not at this juncture still able to look at this and -- you know, I am aware of what you are talking about with respect to the particular raid, but it's still not picturing in my mind where it is. As a result, at the time we did have the casualty -- the daily casualty records of the Bratunac Brigade, we don't have -- or at the time we didn't have the ones for Milici or Skelani separate battalion. I don't recall in this particular context that at any given date the Bratunac Brigade had 13 soldiers killed in a particular raid on 30 June, so, I mean, I rule the Bratunac Brigade out, but I have no way of knowing about the other formations that would have been around the enclave. I can also tell you that given the ERN number range on both the original and the English language translation, I believe that there's a high probability that I would have seen this document. It's got a very early ERN number that's consistent with the same numbers of the Drina Corps -- or the Zvornik and Bratunac material that I was working with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your answer allows for a possibility that the 13 killed may have been civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a possibility, yes, sir. I just don't know the answer, because I don't have the requisite data behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at paragraph number 2. It says that on the 23rd of June, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Zivanovic. I'm taking you back in time to when we handed down our decision on adjudicated facts, and there are these two facts, fact 67 and fact 68, which we decided were to be taken as adjudicated facts and on which we are not going to allow further questions. Fact 67: A raiding party of Bosniaks attacked this nearby Serb village of Visnjica in the early morning of 6th June 1995 and relatively low-intensity attacks. Some houses were burned and several people were killed. Fact 68: Following this attack on Visnjica, the then-commander of the Drina Corps, General Major Milenko Zivanovic, signed two orders on the 2nd of July 1995 laying out the plans for the attack on the enclave and ordering various units of the Drina Corps to ready themselves for combat. The operation was code named "Krivaja 1995". So please no further questions, neither from you nor from anyone else on this, unless there are side issues that haven't been touched upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not be putting any further questions concerning this document, given the decision by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But in your view, was this the reason why the order for combat activities was issued?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was the underlying reason. I believe the underlying reason is reflected in directive 7 and 7-1. This particular raid at this particular time, coupled with the situation on the broader battlefield which made the VRS forces available, may have been the catalyst behind it, but I don't believe that this particular raid, in isolation, was the cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These attacks, coupled with the previous ones, could they have been the reason for making the decision of the 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My analysis reflects the fact that the decision to want to conduct the operations with respect to Srebrenica and Zepa was, again, part of directive 7 and 7-1, something that they would have wanted to do earlier rather than later. The fact that the Bosnian Muslim military forces of both 2 Corps and 1st Corps were engaged in offensive combat operations which tied down a large portion of the mobile forces that the Drina Corps would need either at Mount Majevica or causing forces to be deployed to the Sarajevo battle front precluded that, so my view is that again this is -- this may have been the immediate catalyst because the timing and the availability of forces worked, but I don't believe that this or just the other smaller raids was the underlying cause, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the previous exhibit, the Prosecution Exhibit P107, this being the order for active combat activities. Below the paragraph we referred to, we have units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were at the defence lines of the enclave. Were those units indeed there and were they deployed along the lines as shown in this order? A number of those units carries over to the next page. Therefore, I would kindly ask you to see the following page as well.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it's my understanding that at least in the broad -- in the broad sense that the brigades that are listed were in fact in the enclave. As a component of my analysis and what I was asked to do, I didn't feel it necessary that I had to go back and verify with respect to what the Drina Corps' understanding of where the actual combat lines or combat positions and cross-indexed them to determine whether or not Drina Corps was correct in its analysis of where the enemy forces were located, so I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you conclude from this order that the Drina Corps knew or was familiar with the strength of the forces of Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 2 that you can see on the screen, it states that the goal of the operation was to separate the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and their reduction to the urban parts of the enclaves. In item 4, it says -- rather, it states the lines at which the Serb units should stop or, rather, the lines to which they will advance. It also states the goal, which is to improve the tactical conditions in order to eliminate the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it states that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further down in item 5, we have tasks of the units, and there we can see which units participated in the operation. My question to you, as a military expert, is this: Am I correct in saying that the Drina Corps engaged its best units for this operation or parts of its best units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The goal stipulated here, that is, to separate the enclaves, was achieved on the 9th of July, 1995. I believe you will agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The immediate goal as articulated in this plan would have been achieved by the lines that were achieved on the 9th of July, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at Exhibit P849. You saw this document before, I believe.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in testimony, as well as it's a component of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You believe this document to be an order that was to regulate the continuation of the Krivaja 1995 operation; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of the letter, three tasks are listed. One is to occupy Srebrenica. The other is to disarm the Muslim terrorist gangs, as referred to here. And the third one is to demilitarize the enclave. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's what the paragraph says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is your understanding of the term "Muslim terrorist gangs"? Do you believe it to be the military and paramilitary forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take that to effectively mean the 28th Infantry Division, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this document, I do not see any units that were to participate in the realisation of the goals set out, and I believe you cannot see any either, since it's not in the document. But my question is this: Did you see any other documents which would show what exact units were chosen for the task, what their specific tasks were, and so forth -- so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the Drina Corps, you mean, from the Drina. Yeah. But what's the purpose of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or some other ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the purpose of the question? What are you trying to get from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just his answer, yes or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. As far as I'm aware, the document holdings, we do not have a copy of whatever implementation order was drafted at the IKM that evening which assigned specific units and tasks for the final part, which would be the actual entering of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 12th of July, 1995, a decision was made that the units of the VRS be deployed around Zepa. It is page 19692, lines 1 to 6.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it, but I will agree with your statement, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those units indeed went there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military units that were designated, which were at that time the 2nd -- the elements of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, the elements of the Zvornik Brigade and the elements of the Birac Brigade did, in fact, go there, as well as the other composite units of Milici and the Bratunac Brigade. So those units that were involved in that particular aspect of the Srebrenica operation did, in fact, go to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that concerning the Zepa operation, the very same units were sent there that had participated in the Krivaja 1995 operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, sir, because there were some additional formations of the 65th Protection Regiment that were engaged in that operation, that were not engaged in Srebrenica, as well as of course the southern units of the 1st Podrinje -- or the Rogatica Brigade, as its known, that also did not participate in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, a great number of the units that had participated in the Krivaja-95 operation, for which you said were the best and strongest part of the Drina Corps, were indeed sent to Zepa. Do you agree that they could no longer participate in the implementation of the tasks set out on the 9th of July, 1995, i.e., the disarmament of, as stipulated here, Muslim terrorist gangs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formations that particularly were involved with the takeover of the town of Srebrenica, the tactical group from the Zvornik Brigade, the presumed tactical group from the Birac Brigade and the Romanija Brigade all left the enclave area starting the morning of -- the former enclave starting the morning of 13 July and took the roads from Srebrenica around through the Bracan-Milici area and then to their positions. By taking those routes and by deploying to Srebrenica, those three particular units were not involved in either disarmament activities in Potocari or in combat with respect to the column that occurred on 13 and 14 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim column that was moving from Jaglici and Susnjari starting with the 12th of July early in the morning and onwards, was moving the other way, away from Zepa; can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The large bulk of the column was moving away from Zepa. I understand that some small units, perhaps platoon-sized, did attempt to infiltrate and did in fact make it to Zepa. I believe the number is approximately 200 or 300 people. But given the size of the overall column, you know, it was not a substantial number compared to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, as a military analyst or expert, can you confirm that the Army of Republika Srpska wanted to -- or, rather, had the VRS wanted to kill those people in the column, it would have sent its best and strongest forces towards the column rather than sending them to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I disagree, because I believe that, first of all, as I've testified and as my report reflects, the political factor of General Mladic and the leadership of the RS wanting to very quickly move and take Zepa before the broader international community could react to what had happened at Srebrenica was a key factor. And, in fact, based on statements from individuals that were at that 12 July meeting where the decision was made, that issue was in fact raised, that there was a substantial military threat and it was one that Mladic took into account before he made his decision. So the other factor that is involved and, again, as I've discussed before was that the actual size, particularly on 12 July 1995, the actual size and threat posed by the column was still being consistently underestimated by the leadership of the VRS, Mladic and others on the Main Staff, as well as the Drina Corps. So my view is that, you know, based on the decisions that were taken at the time, the VRS was comfortable, if not overly confident, that the forces that they had arrayed there were sufficient to contain that military threat and to destroy the column. Obviously, in retrospect, knowing the numbers, they were incorrect, but based on the decision that they made and the information they had available, I think it was a fair conclusion that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you say that in spite of the information contained in the order for active combat activities, that Srebrenica should be defended by five brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, that Srebrenica is being defended by five brigades.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and again in light of the fact that, one, there was not clear intelligence or information available to the Main Staff and the Drina Corps on the size and combat power of the column, and it also reflects the fact that there was a considerable body of opinion within the military leadership that, in fact, a large component of the combat power that had come out of Srebrenica was in fact going to go to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you are claiming that in spite of the fact that the best units of the Drina Corps fought for five days to enter Srebrenica, that they did not know the real strength of their enemy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that those units knew and understand the strength of their enemy when they were fighting to go into Srebrenica. I believe that as the military situation and as individuals have -- have come forward later have said that when they arrived in Srebrenica, they found it abandoned, and in military terminology the 28th Infantry Division had successfully managed to break contact with the VRS. As a result of them breaking contact, as a result of the army not knowing where they were, the decision was made that on the 11th of July, the -- I'm sorry, the 12th of July, that the most powerful combat formations that we've just discussed were going to be sent to sweep through the Bardera [sic] Triangle area of the former enclave to engage the enemy. In fact, they swept through empty terrain. So it was a series of miscalculations with respect to the enemy's strength and the enemy intentions that may have played a significant role in the decision by General Mladic to send his best available forces to Zepa rather than to place them along that key intersection to facilitate the complete destruction of the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we'll have a break now, 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Butler, we left it off with the column that was moving from Srebrenica towards Tuzla. Kindly tell me, you must have arrived at the information that at one point, this column represented a serious military threat to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have always testified as such, that the column size was being consistently underestimated during the period of 12 and 13 July and that it did in fact represent a significant military threat to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this threat was even reinforced by the fact that there was very few troops of the VRS in Zvornik at the moment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the -- the documents reflect that the leadership of the Zvornik Brigade at the time - that would be of course Major Obrenovic as the chief of staff - was having considerable difficulty in mustering any available forces to put out in ambush positions to either delay or potentially defeat these enemy formations coming up, because almost all of the reserve manoeuvre forces of the Zvornik Brigade had been tasked to be part of the tactical group led by Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You probably know that mobilisation of all able-bodied men was carried out in Zvornik around the time and that they were involved in the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was in fact orders to mobilize all able-bodied men, military members who were on leave or otherwise not on duty with their units were recalled and sent back to their positions, and the police forces of the public security sector, the SJB for Zvornik, were mobilised in a military company form and were also employed in the defence, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back for the last time to the order for active combat. The number is P107. We will look at bullet point 10(p) on the penultimate page of this document. You also answered some questions by the Prosecutor about this document and about this particular page. The paragraph that I am interested in is on page 5 of the B/C/S version. You're familiar with the second paragraph on page 5, where it says: "The security organs and military police will designate the collection sectors where the prisoners of war and the war booty will be secured." And it says further on that when dealing with prisoners of war and population, the troops have to comply with the Geneva Conventions. You've already testified about that, you must surely remember. I've just shown you this to jog your memory a little, because I'm going to be asking you some questions -- a question about this paragraph. And now I would kindly ask you to look at 1D382. This is the same order for combat activities. The only difference is in the right upper-hand corner, where it says "Copy number 2," whereas the previous order was copy number 3. Now I would kindly ask you to look at the same, the same paragraph number 10, which is again on page number 5. In the B/C/S version -- sorry, in the English version, this should be towards the end of the page, towards the bottom of the page. In the English version, it is towards the bottom of the page, and can you please scroll up the B/C/S version to show the place where we were before. What I need is the previous page of the B/C/S version. Thank you. In this version of the order, you will see that this particular sentence has been crossed out, the sentence which says that: "The security organs and military police will indicate the sectors of collection where prisoners of war will be secured, together with war booty." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see it as being shown in the English version, but in the B/C/S version you can see a line with handwritten text added on the upper margin, with an arrow pointing towards it, and the text reads: "The sector where prisoners of war will be collected is the sector of Pribicevac." I'm not sure whether this is very legible for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The B/C/S page, yeah. [Interpretation] The upper margin of the text, I don't know whether this is visible in the English version. Could you please scroll down -- [In English] Scroll up, sorry. [Interpretation] This part of the text has not been translated, as I can see, but it says here that the sectors for gathering and securing prisoners of war and war booty will be the sector of Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My very short question, to start with, is whether you've seen this document before in this particular version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just to let you know that the translation of those handwritten letters are an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why it is not translated. I cannot see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is, it is, not -- in the main text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the main text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that I've seen this particular B/C/S version of this document, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that in the version that I'm just showing you, the sector for collecting prisoners of war and war booty has been defined and coincides with the tasks that were given to the security organs; in other words, the security organs share with this document that the prisoners of war are not to be their concern and their responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the document is written, with respect to those handwritten scratch-outs that you've mentioned, it's translated as such, and in that any reference to either the security organs or military police has been scratched out, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you must have seen it in the other document that the Prosecutor showed you, which is 3025.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be brought up on the screen. Again, I'm looking for page 5 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, you will find -- just give me a moment to check whether it is indeed on the screen, the third paragraph of the B/C/S version. It should be. It is the third paragraph from the bottom. This is repeated there -- in the English version, I apologise, the third paragraph from the bottom, and it's the third paragraph from the top in the B/C/S, and it says as follows, and this time it has been typed out: "Prisoners of war and war booty will be collected in the Pribicevac sector." Once again, neither the security organs nor the -- have been mentioned. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is what that particular document says. I believe that document is the implementation order from the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As a military expert, could you tell me, please, whether you believe that the security organs were not given the task in order to give them room to focus on their main task, which was counter-intelligence; is that the reason why they were not given this particular task?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given this particular task by whom, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade or the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the document reflecting the Bratunac Brigade, what it says is what it says. Whether or not -- what the intent was behind Colonel Blagojevic, I can't say. He didn't testify, and there was no particular evidence with respect to why it was written the way it was written, if I recall. As for the issue with the Drina Corps, I don't accept your premise that the Drina Corps did not order the security organs to do this. The document that we have from the original Drina Corps order has an origin of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. I do not know the origin of the document that you've shown me that has been scratched out. That leaves one or two -- one of two possibilities. The first possibility is that the Command of the Drina Corps published conflicting sets of orders and guidance with respect to the same military operation and sent them out to different formations, or the other possibility is that the document that you showed me before with the hand cross-outs were hand cross-outs that were in fact not made by the Drina Corps personnel but represent changes in that document that were used then to formulate, you know, lower orders for various units. Again, I don't know the origin of the second document, but certainly from the consistency of language, you know, I believe it's, you know, a fair presumption to say that, you know, the changes in that particular document reflect the changes that were shown in the Bratunac Brigade, it may very well be that they were the ones who made those handwritten changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the information that you are privy to, can you tell me whether you know that in the security organ of the Drina Corps Command, there was anybody else, save for Vujadin Popovic, was there anybody else employed in that organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. My understanding is that Major Golic was with the intelligence organ. I believe at some point in time there was a -- not deputy, but a security referent who would have assisted Colonel Popovic, but I don't recall that that person was available in July of 1995 to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You may be aware of the fact how many people were supposed to be working in that organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- certainly more than one, but I couldn't tell you, off the top of my head, what the organisational formation was for that specific organ, at least as far as the VRS was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I also do not have the formation of the Drina Corps, but I'm going to show you another document from which we might be able to draw some conclusion. The number is 1D647. I don't think the document has been translated. This is an overview of the future and current number of officers in the Command of the Drina Corps. In the first column, there are different departments and divisions of the Command of the Drina Corps. Can you please scroll the document down a little. I have used an arrow to indicate the Department for Intelligence and Security as -- it has been shown here as one department. In the first column is number 9. Number 9 is in the column which shows how many officers should this organ actually have per establishment. Number 9 indicates the number of officers. Number 4 is the number of non-commissioned officers. And the fourth column is the sum of the first two figures. The rest of the table shows the actual situation as it was at the time in the organ, and you can see number 3 indicating that there were three officers, again number 3, which means that the grand total of the officers working in both the intelligence and security organs, according to the information that I have, the three were Vujadin Popovic, Svetozar Kosoric and Pavle Golic. Could you please tell us whether you know if there was anybody else employed in either the intelligence or the security organs at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a date? What do you mean by "the time" or -- in this document? Is there a date, is there more of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid not at the moment. I'll do my best to provide my colleague with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we're talking about the time frame of July 1995, other than the three individuals mentioned, I am aware that there was one other officer present, a lieutenant, whose function was to monitor the collection of -- and information related to intercepted BiH Army communications. I can't recall his name offhand. I believe that he actually -- his name is compromised in some of the intercepts. He was not a security officer, per se. He was somebody who worked out of the intelligence shop. But since this particular number covers all three, I have to say that in July of 1995, you know, using that criteria, you have a total of four.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please confirm that Kosoric and Golic were members of the intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, my understanding is that Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric was the intelligence officer and Major Pavle Golic was also an intelligence officer subordinate to Colonel Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, after these orders that we have just looked at, do you know if anything changed with regard to issuing orders with regard to the prisoners of war after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, obviously something changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D690, please. This is a decision on the appointment of the civilian commissioner for the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica. It was passed on the 11th of July, 1995, by the president of Republika Srpska, Mr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you've seen this decision before.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this decision, Miroslav Deronjic was appointed as the civilian commissioner. Can you now please look at item 4 of this decision, which reads: "The commissioner shall ensure that all civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war and also ensure that the civilian population can freely choose where they will live or move to." Does it arise from this decision that the highest authority with regard to the prisoners of war lay with Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I disagree with that, and I suspect Mr. Deronjic has disagreed with that in the past as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic's reasons are totally understandable to me, but could you please share your reasons with us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- I'm sorry, I'm just fumbling with the volume here because it's a bit annoying. Okay. As noted by the activities of the 12th in Potocari, as well as the activities on the 13th with respect to the taking of prisoners from the column, the practical reality on the ground was that the organs of the armed forces under military command, the VRS command, in Potocari and along the road were those organisations that were dealing with the prisoners at ground level, so they were the ones, you know, at face value, who had responsibility for the prisoners. Whether at some point -- you know, like I said, whether or not at some point it was recognised that Miroslav Deronjic had the ultimate responsibility, I don't know. And certainly from the way that the situation developed afterwards, it doesn't appear that Miroslav Deronjic had any particularly substantive involvement with ensuring that the Geneva Conventions were complied with in this respect with the prisoners of war. So, you know, Miroslav Deronjic does not have authority over the VRS. I mean, General Mladic does. And in that context, you know, the army assumes responsibility for the prisoners that it captures, as well as for the prisoners that the police formations who are under its command captures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this decision made by Radovan Karadzic, who had certain authority over the VRS? Wasn't he the supreme commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 4, it says that: "The commissioner shall ensure that all civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war ..." Can you tell me what it means? What is your interpretation of it, as a military analyst? What is your interpretation of the word "ensure"? How can a civilian commissioner ensure that military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the -- the way that I would read that is that that particular civilian would in fact be charged with monitoring the activities of the army and civilian organs, and when it came to his attention that, with respect to the military, that prisoners were being treated in a way that was not consistent with his instructions, he would be under an obligation to go to the superior officers responsible in the military for this issue and to bring that to their attention. If the military officers and the military failed to make any remedial efforts or actions, his next step would be to bring that situation to the attention of the authorities who are over the head of those particular military ones. So in practical application, you know, if he sees members of the Drina Corps not complying with his instructions, he's obligated to report that fact to General Krstic or whoever the senior Drina Corps person is around. If General Krstic or that senior official does not take remedial action, he's obligated to go to his superior, General Mladic. If that particular person does not take any remedial action, he's obligated to go to General Mladic's superior and inform him, which would be the president of the Republic. That is how I read that particular paragraph to mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this order, it is not said that in case of need, he should report to anyone, in particular General Krstic, Mladic, or anyone of that nature, since he was a civilian commissioner. Do you see this order -- or, rather, do you see this decision by the supreme commander by which the supreme commander transfers very high authority to the commissioner concerning the treatment of prisoners of war ...?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I understand your question, sir. No, there's no specific instructions in paragraph 4 that deal with what I've just discussed. However, as you've noted yourself, he's a civilian commissioner. The appointment as a civilian commissioner does not give him a collateral authority over the armed forces with respect to ordering them what they can and cannot do. Given that particular context, you know, that Miroslav Deronjic can somehow give orders to the army with respect to their treatment of prisoners or how they will handle the prisoners that are in military custody is not what I believe is a fair reading of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Mr. Karadzic, as the president of the Republic and as the supreme commander of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska, and being the highest-position person in the Republika Srpska, could delegate any of his authority to someone else? In other words, are you aware of any regulation that would prevent him from doing so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- you're going to have -- "any authority" is a fairly broad term of art. Could you be a bit more specific, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there is anything in place that would prevent or that would have prevented Mr. Karadzic, as the president of the Republic and the supreme commander of the Armed Forces, to transfer very broad competences to the civilian commissioner regarding the treatment of POWs in the territory of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, it goes back to the VRS Law on Defence and the VRS Law on the Army, circa 1992. Those particular laws regulate the competencies of the army as well as the roles and responsibilities with respect to civilians and what -- what the commander-in-chief can and cannot delegate with respect to authority. And, you know, in part because of my knowledge of those particular laws, that's why, you know, I conclude that an order, you know, as noted in paragraph 4 of this is not to be interpreted as giving Miroslav Deronjic any form of operational control or command over issues that fall within the competence of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree that Mr. Karadzic was not the commander-in-chief? [In English] The commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think that's translated wrong. It says the question is: "You will agree that Mr. Karadzic was not the commander-in-chief?" Was that your correct question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Supreme commander. [In English] Armed Forces of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he was not the commander of the Main Staff, he was in fact the supreme commander which, in the 1992 law, I believe is translated as "Commander-in-chief."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this decision was ever changed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which decision? Are we talking -- was the 1992 law amended at points in time; is that what we're referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the decision on the appointment of Mr. Deronjic to be the civilian commissioner for the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica and his obligation to ensure that the civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that by the end of July 1995, there was a change in the status of Mr. Deronjic reflected in -- in various presidential orders or directives which redesignated him as the war president of the Srebrenica War Presidency by the end of July of 1995. So at some point, these instructions were superseded by additional ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief you were shown another order from the Drina Corps Command, dated the 13th of July, 1995. It is P991. Let us bring it up on the screen, please. In item 3 of the order, it says that captured and disarmed Muslims should be accommodated in appropriate facilities that can be secured with a small number of troops, and to immediately notify the superior command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this order, did you find any obligation of the security organs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could he be allowed to see the entire order, if he's going to be asked that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. [Interpretation] We can move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you are ready, please let us know, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, let's move on to the next page. I was just about to say that. Okay. Yes, sir, I've read the document. Your question again being ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether, in this order, you see any obligations or tasks issued to the security organs.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that there are any specified tasks to the security organs on this one. I believe that the tasks that are listed are -- are general in nature and for the commands and commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief, among others, you also provided answers to certain Prosecutor's questions that had to do with strategic goals of the Serb people, and those goals being published in the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska. I will not invite you to analyse the very contents of the goals. I believe some other Defence teams will busy themselves with that. However, I wanted to ask you this: Do you know or do you recall whether there was a military or international or diplomatic forum or context within which those strategic goals were discussed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the political forum by which those strategic goals were discussed was the assembly meeting of 16 May 1992. So being it was an assembly meeting, it was in fact a political forum, a governmental forum.
