It dealt with not only those strategic goals, but dealt with issues related to the organisation and essentially the adoption of an army and various other aspects, and it also talked about, you know, in the context of the larger series of discussions, you know, the relevant political and strategic situation, yes, sir, as well as the international one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that on the 4th of April, 1992, over a month before that, the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was still part of the SFRY, made a decision on mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I'm willing to agree with the underlying premise of the question, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that a few days later, the same body declared imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the time, there should have been held an international conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina which was supposed to come up with a solution, a political solution for the crisis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that is true or not. That -- that was an issue that was more appropriately researched by other people and not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after the session of the assembly, when the strategic goals were decided upon, and their publication in the Official Gazette, during that one year, that there were negotiations between the international community, on one side, and the different parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the solution for the crisis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am aware of that, at least in the broadest of terms. I can't get into the technical details, because I'm not aware of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you'll be able to answer this, but did you know that the strategic goals were published only once the diplomatic efforts had failed and only once there was no political solution planned that had been adopted; during the entire process of negotiations, the goals were not published?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part I agree, the goals were not published until a point in time when they were, but you're correct, on the other hand, I can't comment as to why they were not published and whether or not that was part of a designed plan for any particular political or international reason. I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't press this matter any further. Mr. Butler, we, as well as you, know that Srebrenica was not demilitarised the way it was envisaged and agreed upon. Therefore, I won't ask you any questions regarding that topic. However, in the course of your analysis and in the course of preparing your reports, did you see how many pieces of weaponry in the period once the enclave had been declared and until it was occupied later, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued to the 28th Division and its military units within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that there are ABiH documents out there that will reflect the gross inventories of weapons of the 28th Division, or before that it was known as Operational Group 8, and I may have seen them. I don't recall any specifically. I certainly don't not doubt that they're out there. I mean, certainly the enclave did have weapons. I just -- like I say, if you want to refresh my memory or show me a document, that's fine, but I don't recall one offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It may not be necessary for me to show you those documents so as not to waste any time concerning the amount of weapons that were distributed. However, I wanted to ask you this: Did you ever, in any document concerning the forwarding of materiel and equipment and ordnance, see that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina distributed its units in Srebrenica food?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The material that was being smuggled into the ABiH -- from the ABiH 2nd Corps over the known over-land smuggling routes would have been, as a function of efficiency, limited to ammunition, documents, weapons, things of that nature. I think it's a fair categorisation to say that the 28th Infantry Division in Srebrenica and, before that, OG-8 depend the on its foodstuff supplies as part of the larger food efforts that were being brought in under the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it called "Human-sharing aid"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the rubric of humanitarian aid, I would generally categorise things such as food, things such as medicine, basic commodity issues potentially with respect to certain clothing items, non-military obviously, or things of that nature. So, yeah, in that respect, the 28th Infantry Division did, in fact, you know, use those humanitarian aid supplies for the sustenance of its military forces, yes, sir. They are referred to in military parlance as dual-use items. They have both military and civilian applications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We heard Major Franken's testimony here. It was between the 17th of October, 2006, page 2446, lines 4 to 14; namely, he said that humanitarian aid that reached the enclave would be put in warehouses. The page of the transcript is 2446; that the humanitarian aid was placed in storage and that it was at the municipal authority's disposal, as well as of UNHCR. The same day, Major Franken said, at page 2538, lines 3 to 11, and page 2642, lines 1 to 4, that the municipality reported to him that the 28th Division keeps taking a part of the UNHCR rations for their needs. He also said that they thought they were so important that they took most of it or a large part of it for themselves. He said that -- he stated the same before the parliamentary commission of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, wait one moment, please. Mr. Zivanovic, what are you trying to prove?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to know if the -- if the witness is aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That the Army of ABiH -- Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina confiscated a part of humanitarian aid from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I take you to our decision on adjudicated facts, fact 50: "Bosnian Muslim helicopters flew in violation of the no-fly zone. The ABiH opened fire towards Bosnian Serb lines and moved through the safe area. The 28th Division was continuously arming itself, and at least some humanitarian aid coming into the enclave was appropriated by the ABiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this has already been taken as an adjudicated fact, and we shouldn't waste more time, unless you wish the witness to contradict it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm actually interested in an answer to another question in relation to this. For you, as a military expert, do you believe that the VRS was supposed to tolerate such supplying of their enemies by humanitarian -- with humanitarian aid which was primarily meant to serve the civilian population of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were they supposed to tolerate it in a military sense? Obviously, the siphoning of humanitarian aid, or any such aid going into the enclave that was being appropriated by the military, the ABiH 28th Division, would substantially increase or at least maintain, you know, the ability of that unit to conduct military operations. So from a military standpoint, the VRS, you know, would see that as detrimental to their purposes. Whether they were supposed to tolerate it or not on a larger scale was a decision whereas presumably, you know, they had to weigh the detriment of maintaining the 28th Infantry Division, you know, in some status, allowing them to be resupplied off of humanitarian aid, versus the issue of whether or not they would be justified in completely constricting off all such aid and the collateral effects it would have on the civilian population in order to degrade the military capabilities of the 28th Division. So it's a very complex set of variables that the VRS had to juggle at that time, and in part not just the VRS, the RS political leadership at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did you ever come by the information that the inhabitants of Srebrenica could not leave Srebrenica without the approval of the civilian and military authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina that existed in the enclave? Would you agree with that, if I made -- if I put it to you this way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that there is information available, and I've seen it, that reflects that the -- not only the Srebrenica but also the Zepa enclave, that there are specific instructions that civilians are not to leave those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As a military expert, I would like to ask you the following: The authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did they want to keep the population in order to make the population the human shield for the activities of the 28th Division that were undertaken from the enclave, because if the population had left, those units would have remained unprotected?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether, in a strictly military sense, the human shield applicability is fully accurate, only in as much that there is also the political justification that was used by the ABiH leadership that the presence of the civilian population there, you know, their primary motivator was in fact, because of that civilian population, that the United Nations -- UN protection forces would be deployed there to, in fact, create a buffer between the two forces. If -- your hypothetical would make sense if there were in fact no international forces providing that role, and then it could very well be looked at as that type of a calculated decision. But you have that third international party in there, so in this context I believe that, you know, the ABiH government wanted the population to remain in there in order to continue the justification for having the UN maintain those safe areas, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to the intercepts, another area that you have spoken about at great length. In answering questions about the intercepts, you said that as a military professional, you were aware of the fact that you might be misled on purpose with all that material, that this could have all been misinformation. The way I understood you, you said that during your career, you also had experience in the area of radio communication?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. I think my -- okay, my microphone is back. I'm sorry. Yes, sir, I do have, as part of my military career, some experience in processing and analysing that information, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the technical aspects of the job or were you only involved in analysing the information obtained through radio communication?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, sir. The -- as a function of the analytical practice of my particular branch, and as I believe I've discussed before, you know, part of evaluating the accuracy of the material is also understanding how the information was in fact collected, to ensure that the material that you are looking at, you know, could in fact be collected and again, as the first part, was authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about radio communication, would that imply radio relay communication as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it falls under that same broad category.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The intercepts that you had an occasion to see, you found them reliable and authentic. At least this is what you said in answering the Prosecutor's questions, as far as I could understand.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they're authentic in so much as the fact that they are -- you know, they are and were at the time within the capabilities of the ABiH to collect that material, and the fact that the material that is listed in the various notebooks, printouts, and I believe there are a few audiotapes that have been discussed, you know, is a reflection of that, reliable in fact so much -- reliable with respect to that the processes that the collectors were using to write down the information, and to process that information with respect to what they were doing with it at a collection point, not analysing it, in a broader sense, were reliable. The question of reliability as to the actual intelligence information that can be gleamed from the intercept itself, in fact -- you know, its reliability is in part determined by whether or not the individuals who were being intercepted, you know, know what they're talking about. So we do have to be careful with the phrase "reliability." I mean, the fact that you can get a perfectly valid intercept of a communication, you know, and it may be perfectly accurate and reliable, in that sense, doesn't in fact mean that the information that the two correspondents are talking about corresponds to reality. I know it's a technical parsing-out of phrases, but that's why I always steer away from the idea that, you know, reliability, you know, can cover all of those bases. I believe each intercept has to be looked at on an individual basis and individual judgements and determination of reliability on those intercepts have to be based, you know, on the context of other things as they're occurring at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Given your experience in the area, you must be familiar with some standard procedures that are applied when intercepting radio communication. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean with reflect to "standard procedures." I mean, I'm aware of the procedures of my own military. I can't comment as to whether or not other militaries followed similar procedures, whether they followed different procedures. I mean, I can tell you that, you know, while it was an extraordinarily low technical approach that the ABiH did to collect this information, my own -- with my own background and the research that I did with respect to their abilities, you know, I do conclude that, you know, while low tech, they were more than technically capable of collecting the information that they collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And from the material that you had available, I'm sure that you could familiarise yourself with the procedures that the BiH Army applied.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm whether the collection of this information is actually part of the intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material that we have, with respect to those from ABiH 2 Corps, as well as from the 24th Division, were part of, as I understand it, their intelligence branch. I am aware that some of the other intercepts originated from intelligence bodies that were outside of the control of the ABiH military, and they were in fact civilian or Ministry of the Interior. I believe the categorisation was "AID" at the time. So I hope that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does, thank you. And can you also confirm that intercepting such communication is carried out in order to obtain information about the enemy strength and the enemy intentions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a broad sense, yes, sir. That would be why they would be doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And with that goal in mind, this information is then conveyed to the superior commands?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that the BiH Army had had technical capabilities to intercept the radio communication of the VRS Army, had you been able to establish that based on some technical documentation or technical information that was available to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with respect to the intercepts that we have that cover the Drina Corps and VRS, you know, multichannel relay communications backbone, as well as what are known as the tactical intercepts, which are the radio intercepts that cover the short-range VHF transmitters, what I was able to do early on is, looking at various Drina Corps communication plans that we had seized as part of the Zvornik seizure, you know, lay out some of those communications plans and annexes. And I was able to, while not exactly parse through frequencies and things of that nature, you know, get a general appreciation that the VRS backbone communications relay sites and systems as it existed and what the ABiH 2nd Corps people thought they were intercepting were consistent, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We've heard a number of witnesses here who have spoken about that and who worked on that, and they have explained the procedure to us, in short terms. This -- they have spoken about the technical aspects of inspecting radio communication. I don't know whether you have the same information, so I'm going to give you some of the details, and I will kindly ask you just to confirm whether what you know is the same as what we know. We heard that the BiH Army operators recorded the conversations on audiotapes. Do you have the same information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding is that during the initial process, the conversations were in fact audiotaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We've also heard that the conversations that had been audiotaped were then transcribed and then sent to the superior command in the form of reports. Would you be able to confirm that this is also what you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that's generally consistent with the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on, we -- we've been told that the audiotapes, once they were full, were also sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, my understanding was that the standard practice, at least with respect to the ABiH 2 Corps sites, was that because there was a shortage of audiotapes, many of the sites in fact, once they had fully transcribed the conversations necessary, used those tapes over again. While I suspect some -- or, you know, a few may have been sent up, because ultimately we do have audiotapes, you know, I do understand that the practice was, for the most part, that they would re-use the audiotape over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, it's not our intention to stop you, by any means, but we are all wondering why you're dealing with these details in relation to intercepts with this witness when you had every opportunity, and you did, actually, deal with the persons who were in a much better position to inform us on the procedure. Anyway, if you want to keep on going, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because this witness testified that ABiH was capable, that he established that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and he's confirming it, thanks to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'd just like to see the scope of his investigation regarding the instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. We're not going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've told us that you didn't know that the tapes were sent to the Command once they were full. Could you please share with us the source of different information, or maybe it would be best for me to share with you the statement of a witness to whom we refer as PW-130, who has told us that the tapes would be sent to the Command, listened to, and then the most important conversations were re-recorded on different tapes, and then the second set of tapes were stored, whereas the first set of tapes were re-sent to the units after the conversation had either been erased from them or not, in which case the units would make sure that the tapes were re-useable by erasing the first set of conversations, would -- are you familiar with this? Is that the information that you might have?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't -- I don't have that information. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the spring of 1998, were you in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time when these tapes were found, i.e., when part of that intercept material was handed over to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Clarify that. That's very different information in the same question, those are all different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're right, but I think Mr. Butler can make some sense of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall being in Bosnia in the spring of 1998 and dealing with ABiH 2 Corps officers who were giving us some of those tapes that they had, in company with Mr. Jack Hunter, I believe. Whether it was part of the same mission or a different mission again in the spring of 1998, I recall being up at one of the particular intercept sites where we came across a number of the actual notebooks. So in general terms, I recall what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And obviously on that occasion, you requested for the tapes to be handed over?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't request. The request, of course, was made by the leader of the investigation, and the investigation, you know, once we became aware of the tapes, we did request that they be turned over to the Office of the Prosecutor. There was a process that had to be followed where the ABiH 2 Corps had to get approval from Sarajevo to do so. I think on the subsequent mission, when we returned, that they had in fact received that information, and the OTP took custody of 14 audiotapes, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you still agree with me that only one or two tapes referred to the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. Because I don't speak the language, I didn't sit there and listen to all the tapes or a streaming transcript. I mean, I know that the tapes cover in some cases, you know, 1995, from the beginning portions of it, that they're not a complete record of all of the intercepts, so, I mean, I couldn't give you a ballpark figure on how many of the tapes only deal with issues related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You must be aware of the fact that the intercepts and the intercepted material were first requested in 1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know that. I wasn't here at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not hear that when you joined the Tribunal, that the intercepts had already been on request from 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. When I first joined the investigative team with respect to supporting them, and my initial discussions with Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, you know, he had indicated that they had information that there were intercepts available primarily because the Bosnian government had released some transcripts of some intercepts and they were being made in -- you know, they were in the local press, and that they had been requested. But I'm not aware that that request went all the way back to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You, as a military analyst or, rather, expert, did you find it strange that you received the intercept material three years after the event?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly strange in so much as, as I've come to learn the various governmental procedures, particularly after the war in Bosnia, nothing happens fast, and also as our own efforts and investigation revealed, even by 1997 and 1998, when we were trying to acquire this information, it was clear that the Bosnian government didn't themselves have a full handle on all of the different people who might have had this material and have it centralised. Would I have liked it, you know, to have been available sooner or later? I mean, obviously everyone wants to get it immediately for whatever reasons it's going to be used, but what political drivers that the military and the civilian leadership in Bosnia used or did not use to make their decision and release it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I would kindly ask you to have a look at 1D12. It's a statement given by the chief investigator, Mr. Ruez, concerning the retrieval of intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, so no broadcast, because this document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a hard copy, if necessary. Maybe that will be speedier, to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's already on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To explain it briefly to you, this is Jean-Rene Ruez's statement in which he provides his experience in the requests for intercept material. Please direct your attention to paragraph 3, in which it is said that: "During the summer 1995, the question was raised with AID ...", the question of intercepts collected by the 2nd Corps of the BiH. It also states that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness has already read it. You're taking much longer than anyone who would need to read that paragraph, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at the penultimate sentence of the paragraph, where it says that: "Through the same means the answer consistently confirmed the existence of these intercepts, but that the timing for a request of access was not appropriate." You, as a military analyst, what would be your interpretation of this answer, which acknowledges that such intercepts are in existence, but however that the time is not right to request them and that the same request was being made throughout 1995, 1996 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you exactly what it was, and let's keep in mind, you know, a little perspective on this particular issue. With respect to the intercepts and our abstract use of them within the court and within the investigation, you know, we're talking about information that may become evidence. In the real world, that was Bosnia from 1995 to 1996 and 1997, what the Office of the Prosecutor was asking the government of Bosnia to do was to essentially compromise a significant wartime and even peacetime intelligence collection capability that would essentially reveal how extensive and successful their intelligence operations had been not only against the VRS but, by definition, you know, or by extension, how successful they had been against the HV -- or HVO -- and HVO, as well as the United Nations and other such agencies. I have no doubt in my mind that within the government, there must have been some significant push-back with respect to discussions as to whether or not the providing of this information to the Office of the Prosecutor, in the interests of justice, you know, would have outweighed at the time their legitimate security concerns with respect to protecting a valuable source of information. I mean, what we were asking at the time, and I'm not -- like I said, I didn't get here until 1997, but, you know, during this period what we were asking for was essentially unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't you think it's time to move to another subject, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Such a reply, could it raise doubts with you, as a military analyst, as to whether that material was yet to be made up in the following period, and that that was the reason why the request was not approved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you're exactly right, and I believe I've testified extensively that that was my primary concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to show you but one statement, or rather it's an information report drafted during the March 1998 mission. It is an interview with one of the operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move into private session for that, just for a brief period of time, please. It is 1D577.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at another exhibit, but before that, tell me this, please: Would you agree that out of the intercepts you listened to, you did not encounter a single one that would have to do with June 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I can -- either June of 1995 or -- I mean, the intercepts that I listened to, because I -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. July 1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I don't understand the language, my purpose of listening to the audiotapes that we had, or copies of them, was strictly limited to my attempt to get a feel, for lack of a better word, as to a lot of the intangibles that I understand go into radio traffic, issues of static, issues of mechanical switching devices. Multichannel radio communications have a peculiar way of demodulating slightly when they drop up and down in frequency a bit. You know, as part of my own effort to look at these and determine whether or not what we were actually listening to was multichannel communications or, you know, tactical-level VHF communications, which have their own things. So, again, I am aware that at least one audiotape had something related to at least Zepa at the end of July 1995, because that was a potential exhibit in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us have a look now at 1D218. It is a letter of the State Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 24th of July, 1995. It is very brief. I am not sure whether this has been translated, although it had been requested. It is very brief. I'll read it out to you. In it, a request was made of the 2nd Corps -- well, it reads: "Given that in the latest offensive against the protected area of Srebrenica, the aggressor committed genocide over the Bosniak people. We kindly ask you that you require all phono material, audio material, pertaining to Srebrenica, from the assistant chief for security. The audio material is needed in order to open a file that will be put at the disposal of the International Tribunal in The Hague." My question is this: Did you ever see this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't recall that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For you, as the expert, would this raise any doubts if even after such a request, the tapes with alleged conversations would be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean it would -- it would continue to, you know, be a piece of the weighting of information particularly with respect to my work on the intercepts, that, you know, would have continued to keep in the front of my mind that I always had to be aware of the material that I was working with that had been provided by these measures were a form of disinformation or deception, yes, sir. I had that in the front of my mind going in, and this piece of information would have just continued to pour weight on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In order to save time, I will not show you some other requests requiring that such audio material be forwarded. Those documents had the same goal in mind. However, I will show you a reply by the intelligence administration of the General Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, sent on the 7th of June [as interpreted] 1996 to the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is 1D221. The date is the 7th of July, 1996. To remind ourselves, at that time, according to Mr. Ruez's statement, the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina were saying that they did have the intercepted conversations, but that the time was not right for them to be delivered or, rather, that access be granted. I am quite positive that we do have a translation of this document. Since it seems that the translation is not appearing, although I am certain that we have it and it was put in e-court, it was actually exhibited, I just wanted to tell you that this refers to the information which, until July 1996 -- or by July 1996, was in possession of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their counter-electronic warfare section. The first paragraph states: "Pursuant to your request, we ran a check and research of most of the information that had been gathered during the period of occupation of Srebrenica and Zepa. We established which units of the aggressor participated in the occupation and crimes. We also determined the names of those who were in any way engaged during the occupation operations, be it by commanding and controlling directly or by taking immediate part in it. In addition to the names of those people, we also mention specific parts of information that we have at our disposal, their participation, and nature of engagement. Most of the information was gathered by electronic reconnaissance, and the audio documentation had been forwarded earlier, back in 1995, pursuant to a request made by the Agency for Research and Documentation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that the Intelligence Administration of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not have the original documents that may be used as valid proof in a court proceeding." I won't read out the whole document, but the page continues listing the units which participated in the operations, and then what follows is the names of individuals, and for that we'll have to go to the next page. Please have a look at the names mentioned and tell me whether, among those names, you see the name of Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had a question which you took three minutes to read, and now we have a list which anyone can read and come to a conclusion whether your client is listed or not. Do you have to ask the question and get the information from a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't finish. The examination of my client got in this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you could have gone straight to this list. You suggest to the witness that your client is not listed there and ask for an explanation, if that is what you want. This is why you asked for five hours, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not -- all right. It was not main point of my question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go to your main point, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm expecting the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do not let the witness tell us whether your client is included in this list --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- if we can see it for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you go through the rest of the document for yourself, and you'll see that specific conversations are referred to, starting with the 3rd of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rest of the document, that if the witness is seeing what I am seeing, it is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just the dates are relevant in the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Then go straight to your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you go through the document, please, so as to be able to see the dates? Just the dates. Please stop there. Can you see a single conversation between the 12th and the 19th of July, 1995? We can go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I confess that you have me at a bit of a disadvantage here, not understanding the language. I see date time hacks that I recognise because they're in Latin, but I can't tell you what the context is. I mean, it doesn't appear to be a conversation in so much as the way that the OTP has translated conversations, but I don't know what I'm looking at, sir, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will have a translation of this for you, and perhaps you will be able to answer some of my questions then.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you are familiar with the devices used by the VRS in July 1995, and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was intercepting the conversations made via those devices?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that these are RUR-1 and RUR-800?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I am familiar with the 800 devices, which are the high-end, multichannel ones. I think the -- to make sure I'm not confusing it with the RU-12, which are the VHF ones, the RU-1s are the low end or what we would call low-end frequency UHF multichannel. They don't have the same extensive bandwidth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the radio relay frequency modules used by the RUR-800 devices?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very broad terms, the ranges, but, I mean, I couldn't give you frequency numbers off the top of my head, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see the frequency plans of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documents that we primarily use with respect to the Zvornik Brigade, which we had seized first, and to the Bratunac Brigade, I am not aware that there was a specific frequency plan with those documents. I don't know, having not gone through the entire Drina Corps material, the new stuff, whether or not there is a frequency plan for each of those networks in that, so the short version is: No, I have not seen a frequency plan for the radio relay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the March 1998 mission, you had an interview with one of the participants. 1D232 is the number of the document that I'm kindly asking you to look at.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Don't broadcast, please. And if they have broadcast it, let me redact -- okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, it says, finally: [In English] "Changed either the operating frequencies of the channel designations of the network. This allowed the BiH to fine tune their collection to both specific relay stations and to specifically target channels which were dedicated to commanders and key staff officers." [Interpretation] Did you ever hear such an explanation provided by this person? I believe that -- actually, there's no need for me to mention the person's name, because you will find it in the next paragraph. He was not a protected witness, but there is really no need for me to spell out his name.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what -- did I hear the explanation provided by this person? Yeah, I'm familiar with that explanation, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that your information also, that the frequencies didn't change?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean, "was that your information also"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive this type of information from somebody else to the same effect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go back to the first page of this document, please, sir. At the time that this document was written, we were still indexing through all of the material that we had seized from both Bratunac and Zvornik and hadn't begun to significantly do that type of analytical work yet as part of the intercepts. You'll notice that, you know, while the date of the memo is 18 December, you know, and the actual meeting occurred on the 5th of March, 1998. At that point in time, I don't think we even had -- we had the documents yet. So what is in this text here is what the individual told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you don't know exactly how many features participated in the radio relay communication via RRU-800, and I'm talking about July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean by "features"? It could be a translation error, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many objects were on the radio relay or else that were involved in the communication between Vlasenica and Zvornik, to be more precise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 05 March 1998 when I discussed this issue with him, and when we wrote it up on 18 December 1998, that information was not available to me. My purpose behind this was strictly to get an accounting of what the individual was saying. At that time, I had no material ability to either confirm or deny the information, and I didn't, myself, have an appreciation of what the VRS communications architecture was in that region. We had no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you evaluated the authenticity of the material that you received with regard to the intercepted conversations, did you take into account all these frequencies and did you make your own evaluation as to whether these conversations could have actually taken place at the places as denoted in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that was a fundamental component of my work in attempting to authenticate that body of information not only, like I said, to the satisfaction of the Trial Chamber, but also in the Krstic case and the Blagojevic case, as well as for use in my own reports. That's why I worked with that particular information, in order to make sure that it was in fact what it was purported to be before I would use it as a component of my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell me which elements you used in order to be able to establish that the conversations of the VRS could be intercepted at these locations? You've told us that you didn't know whether there was any frequency plan at the moment.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were going through the material from the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, one of the most useful documents that we found, from a beginning point of view, was a document that was essentially called "Shield-95." It was an operation -- it was a very large detailed operations plan that the VRS had drafted for the post-Dayton environment. One of the annexes to this plan was a rather detailed communication annex which led out and gave us the schematic of the backbone of the VRS communications in that particular area of the country. Now, granted it was in November of 1995, but it gave us, analytically, a starting point to then go backwards in time with the, you know, goal of either confirming or denying that the locations remain valid and the systems and capabilities remain valid. I mean, the next step is we went through the drill of once the documents, in large respect, had set up the context of where the military units were, you know, looking over the broader body of the intercepts - and again I took them in one entire batch for the month of July when they were done, I didn't do this piecemeal - to determine how they overlaid contextually with the situation on the ground that was being portrayed by the military documents of the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade. As a general rule, I could at least move forward with a high degree of confidence that the ABiH 2 Corps, as well as the AID and other agencies that were collecting that material, you know, didn't have access to those military documents. As such, they would provide a very meaningful and fair check by which we could then cross-index the intercepts to. That was a continual process over time as we developed -- as we developed the analytical picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that when searching the premises of the Zvornik Brigade, you came by the communication plan of the VRS, does that mean that you also obtained the frequency plan for the RRU-800 communication at the same time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't say that we came across the -- the communication plan that we came across in Zvornik was "Shield-95". I don't believe that the Stit-95 plan had an associated frequency plan with it. It just indexed out the network. It didn't have frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [In English] ... If you permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My cross-examination is not concluded. I have another topic, and there is just two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll continue tomorrow. We can stop here. We'll continue tomorrow. There is a redaction that you will get notified of in due course. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Butler, I think you can leave. Thank you. And we'll reconvene tomorrow morning as well, I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 9.00. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not familiar with Mr. Butler's -- well, this week I know Mr. Butler's schedule. The following week, we may need to check with him or someone else to see. He may have court --
